You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: every wrong submission costs 1 and every demo request costs 1. An
instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt cap is reached, and
reaching the cap is charged the full cap. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

# Continual-ARC inference and interaction

Use for interactive Continual-ARC instances with a test grid, demonstration requests, and scored submissions.

## Protocol first

- On every turn, provide exactly one action JSON object on the last line: `{"action":"submit","grid":[...]}`, `{"action":"request_demos"}`, or `{"action":"finish"}`. Do not add prose or unrelated tool calls to puzzle turns.
- `finish` is only appropriate after the instance is over. Keep dimensions and cell values valid (rows/columns 1–30, values 0–9).
- Demonstration requests and wrong submissions have explicit costs. Use received evidence carefully; request another demo when it can resolve genuine ambiguity, rather than reflexively requesting or guessing.

## Infer from observed differences

1. Parse the entire input/output demo pair and identify exact cell changes, objects, colors, and spatial relationships. Distinguish unchanged elements from transformed ones.
2. Compare multiple demonstrations when available. Prefer the narrowest rule that explains all examples, including which components are preserved and how edge cases behave.
3. Do not assume a loaded ARC skill applies just because it is familiar; use its rule only when the observed demo supports it. In particular, do not infer stamping from a grid containing compact colored shapes and markers alone.
4. When the rule is underdetermined, request a demo specifically to distinguish plausible hypotheses. Avoid a low-information demo if a confident rule is already established.
5. Apply the inferred transformation to the test grid, preserving everything not implicated by the rule. Validate dimensions, row lengths, and that each changed cell follows the inferred rule before submitting.

## Pitfalls

- Treat the whole grid as evidence: templates, isolated markers, large patterns, and background may have different roles. A compact shape may be a distractor or part of some other relation.
- A single demo can leave the changed object or mapping unclear; compare input and output directly rather than relying on visual intuition.
- Keep output to the required action JSON. ## Validated partition-and-count rule (task-184e66d7)
Two demonstrations established a compact summary transformation: full-width horizontal dividers and/or full-height vertical dividers partition the grid into rectangular panels. Each panel contains a background color and isolated cells of one marker color. Output one cell per panel, preserving the panel layout/order; use output marker color 1 exactly for panels containing two marker cells, and use the input background color for panels with any other count. ## Paired bars project a scattered marker pattern (task-345ec273)
Two equal-length, same-color bars embedded in the background can define the ends of rows to complete. In the demonstrations, one bar was vertical at a grid edge in an upper/lower region and the other bar occupied corresponding rows/columns in another region; isolated marker-color cells between/near the bars determined which row offsets to draw.
